Q1Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterUnits and Measurements high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on expressing a distance in a new system of units where c = 1, so distance = c x t = 400 new units, which is conversion of units / choice of system of units.
subtopic 1System of Units
why this subtopicThe answer depends on reading the new system of units in which c = 1, so the unit of length is the distance light covers in 1 s and the Sun-Earth distance is just the travel time 400 s expressed as 400 new units.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The speed of light in vacuum is taken as unity. If light takes 6 min 40 s to reach the Earth from the Sun, the distance between the Sun and the Earth in new unit is:
  1. 3 × 108
  2. 500
  3. 3 × 1010
  4. 400
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. Time, t = 6 min 40 s
  2. = 360 + 40
  3. = 400 s
  4. Distance in new system d = vt
  5. = 1 × 400 = 400

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Convert the travel time: t = 6 min 40 s = 6 × 60 + 40 = 400 s.
  2. In the new system the speed of light is unity, so c = 1 distance-unit per second.
  3. d = c t = 1 × 400 = 400 new units, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultymedium · 2 steps
stepsChange 6 min 40 s into seconds. It is 400 s. → In this new system c = 1. Distance = c x t. So the distance in new units is the same number as the time in seconds.
confusing options2 of 4 · options 4, 2
400 is what the time printed in this question gives you. 500 is the number you have memorised for sunlight reaching Earth, because that trip takes 8 min 20 s, which is 500 s. So 500 is where you land if you answer from memory instead of reading the 6 min 40 s given here.
why it is trickyThere is only one step. But the paper changed a number you already know. Sunlight takes 8 min 20 s, which is 500 s. Here the question says 6 min 40 s, which is 400 s. If you answer from memory you pick 500. If you read the question you pick 400. The other two numbers, 3 x 108 and 3 x 1010, are just speed-of-light values. Once c = 1, no working leads to them.
the catchThis is a memory trap, not a maths mistake. You have to notice that the question changed the usual number. You also have to see that c = 1 makes the answer the same number as the time in seconds.

Q2Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterMechanical Properties of Solids high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the defining formulae of Young's modulus, bulk modulus, compressibility and Poisson's ratio, the elastic moduli taught in mechanical properties of solids.
subtopic 1Hooke's Law
why this subtopicThe answer depends on the defining formulae of the elastic moduli - Young's modulus FL/A(dL), compressibility, bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio - which are the elastic constants introduced with Hooke's law.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Match List I with List II:

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
A.Young's ModulusI.Δ dΔ L(Ld)
B.CompressibilityII.FLA(Δ L)
C.Bulk ModulusIII.-1Δ P(Δ VV)
D.Poisson's RatioIV.-P(VΔ V)
  1. A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III
  2. A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV
  3. A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II
  4. A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. A. Young's Modulus = StressStrain = FLAΔ L
  2. B. Compressibility = 1Bulk modulus = -1Δ P(Δ VV)
  3. C. Bulk Modulus = -P(VΔ V)
  4. D. Poisson's Ratio = Lateral strainLongitudinal strain = Δ dΔ L(Ld)

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Young's modulus is longitudinal stress over longitudinal strain: Y = F/AΔ L/L = FLA Δ L, which is II, so A-II.
  2. Compressibility is the reciprocal of bulk modulus: k = 1B = -1Δ P(Δ VV), which is III, so B-III.
  3. Bulk modulus is B = -Δ PΔ V/V = -P(VΔ V), which is IV, so C-IV.
  4. Poisson's ratio is lateral strain over longitudinal strain: σ = Δ d/dΔ L/L = Δ dΔ L(Ld), which is I, so D-I.
  5. A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultyeasy · 4 steps
stepsSpot FL/A(dL). This is Young's modulus. → Spot -(1/dP)(dV/V). This is compressibility. → Spot -P(V/dV). This is bulk modulus. → Spot (dd/dL)(L/d). This is Poisson's ratio.
confusing options1 of 4 · option 4
Only one option matches A with II. And FL/A(dL) is the one formula here that you can name straight away. So the three options that start with A-IV, A-III and A-I are gone on the first row.
why it is trickyOn paper there are four things to recall. But the options end it after the first one. Once you name Young's modulus, three options go. The slip that would really hurt is swapping compressibility with bulk modulus, because they are reciprocals. That swap is not printed in any option that survives the A row.

What catches a student
The trapoption 3Reversedreversedthe right thing stated backwards: direction, order or ratio

Compressibility is the reciprocal of the bulk modulus, and that sentence alone does not say which of the two printed volume expressions is the reciprocal one, so the pair gets handed over inverted. B-IV with C-III is printed only in option 3, so one inversion carries the whole code.

Who fallsa student who has learnt compressibility as 1/K but recalls only the pair, not which side carries Δ P in the denominator

Why it feels rightIII and IV are built from the same two quantities, Δ P and Δ V/V, and both carry a minus sign, so either one reads as the volume modulus

  1. okIII and IV are the only expressions built from pressure and volume, so they belong to Compressibility and Bulk Modulus.
  2. bad-P(VΔ V) has Δ V underneath, so take it as the compressibility and give III to the bulk modulus.Compressibility is volume strain *per unit* pressure, so pressure is the divisor: III is compressibility and IV is the bulk modulus.
Also pullsoption 1

Who fallsa student who reads F/A as a pressure and files any pressure-over-strain expression under the bulk modulus

Why it feels rightII opens with force over area, and the modulus taught in the words 'pressure divided by strain' is the bulk modulus

  1. okFLA(Δ L) is F/AΔ L/L, a stress divided by a strain.
  2. badThat stress is a pressure, so the expression is the bulk modulus, giving C-II, which only option 1 carries.The strain in it is Δ L/L, a change in length; the bulk modulus divides by a volume strain Δ V/V, so II is Young's modulus.
No route to itoption 2

Checked all four of its pairs against the printed symbols: it gives Young's Modulus the pressure-volume expression III, Compressibility the force expression II, Bulk Modulus the length-ratio expression I and Poisson's Ratio the pressure expression IV, so every pair places an expression on a quantity that shares none of its symbols. The two pairs printed only in option 2, A-III and B-II, each require ignoring the one symbol that identifies the expression -- Δ V in III and F/A in II -- so no partial reading of a printed expression selects this code.

Q3Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterSemiconductor Electronics high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on deciding which ideal diodes are forward biased and therefore conduct, which is diode circuit behaviour taught with the semiconductor diode.
subtopic 1PN Junction Diode Under Forward Bias
subtopic 2PN Junction Diode Under Reverse Bias
why this subtopicThe answer 15/2 A depends on seeing that only the forward-biased branches (4 ohm and 2 ohm) conduct as ideal shorts while the reverse-biased branches (3 ohm, 5 ohm) carry no current, giving R = 4/3 ohm across 10 V.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The current I in the circuit shown below is: (All diodes are ideal and identical)
  1. 53 A
  2. 59 A
  3. 13 A
  4. 152 A
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. For ideal diode, forward resistance = 0 and reverse biased resistance = ∞
  2. ∴ Circuit can be redrawn as,
  3. I = 102 + 104
  4. = 304 = 152 A

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. The battery's + plate feeds the left rail, so conventional current leaves it upward (as the arrow I shows) and crosses every branch from left to right.
  2. A diode conducts only when its arrowhead points along the current, i.e. to the right: that is true for the 4 Ω branch and the 2 Ω branch.
  3. The diodes in the 3 Ω and 5 Ω branches point left, so they are reverse biased and those branches carry no current.
  4. The two conducting branches are in parallel: Req = 4 × 24 + 2 = 43 Ω.
  5. I = VReq = 104/3 = 304 = 152 A, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsCheck each ideal diode. Is it forward biased or reverse biased? → Replace every conducting diode with a plain wire. Replace every reverse biased diode with a break in the circuit. → Simplify the resistors that are left and use Ohm's law to find I.
confusing options2 of 4 · options 1, 2
5/3 A and 5/9 A come from the same battery voltage divided by two different total resistances. Each one is what you get from a different guess about which diodes conduct. So the whole question is the choice between those two guesses.
why it is trickyThe method is standard and quick to plan. The only work that separates 5/3 from 5/9 is checking the bias of each diode. If you assume every diode conducts, you still land on a printed option, not on a strange number. So a wrong assumption never warns you.
the catchDiode circuits punish you if you simplify the resistors before you check the bias. The wrong options come from wrong guesses about which diodes conduct. They do not come from arithmetic slips.

Q4Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterRotational Motion medium confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on rotational kinematics for a rigid body spinning up at constant angular acceleration, average angular speed x time giving 150 revolutions.
subtopic 1Angular Velocity and Angular Acceleration
why this subtopicThe answer depends on uniformly accelerated angular motion - the revolutions equal the mean angular speed (600+1200)/2 rpm times 10 s, i.e. 150 revolutions.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The angular speed of a flywheel is increased from 600 rpm to 1200 rpm in 10 s. The number of revolutions completed by the flywheel during this time is:
  1. 900
  2. 600
  3. 150
  4. 300
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. α = ω2 - ω1Δ t = (1200 - 60010)2π60 = 2π rad/s2
  2. ⇒ Use equation of motion, ω22 = ω12 + 2αθ
  3. ⇒ ω2 = 1200 × 2π60 = 40π
  4. ω1 = 600 × 2π60 = 20π
  5. (40π)2 = (20π)2 + 2 × 2πθ
  6. ⇒ 1200 π2 = 4πθ
  7. ⇒ θ = 300π radian
  8. ⇒ Number of revolution = θ2π = 150

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. Convert both rates to revolutions per second: n1 = 60060 = 10 rev/s and n2 = 120060 = 20 rev/s.
  2. With uniform angular acceleration the mean rate is n = n1 + n22 = 10 + 202 = 15 rev/s.
  3. N = n t = 15 × 10 = 150 revolutions, which is option 3.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
33 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsFind the average speed: (600 + 1200)/2 = 900 rpm → Change it to turns per second: 900/60 = 15 rev/s → Multiply by 10 s to get the number of turns.
confusing options2 of 4 · options 3, 4
300 is what you get if you forget to halve. You add 600 and 1200, convert, then multiply by 10. That answer is printed, so the one slip this question is built to catch has a home.
why it is trickyThree short steps with a formula you know. But option 4, 300, is the average taken without halving. So everything depends on one factor of two inside a method you already have. Option 1, 900, is the average rpm itself. It tempts you only if you stop before converting. It is a weaker trap, because rpm is not a number of turns.
the catch300 is exactly what you get if you forget the 1/2 in the average angular speed. Nothing later in the question catches that slip.

Q5Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterOscillations high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the kinetic energy of a simple harmonic oscillator varying as cos^2, hence repeating with period T/2 and never going negative.
subtopic 1Energy Conservation in SHM
why this subtopicThe answer depends on the kinetic energy of an oscillator varying as cos^2(wt), so K.E. is non-negative and repeats with period T/2 rather than T.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
For a simple pendulum, having time period T, the variation of kinetic energy (K.E.) with time (t) is represented by:
  1. drawn by the pipeline from a figure spec
  2. drawn by the pipeline from a figure spec
  3. drawn by the pipeline from a figure spec
  4. drawn by the pipeline from a figure spec
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. Kinetic energy, K = 12mv2
  2. = 12mA2ω2cos2(ω t + φ)
  3. ∴ K ∝ cos2(ω t + φ)

→ the working concludes: unclear

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: unsure · low
  1. For a simple pendulum the bob's speed is v = Aωcos(ω t + φ), so K.E. = 12mA2ω2cos2(ω t + φ).
  2. cos2 has period πω = T2, so the K.E. curve repeats twice per oscillation and never goes negative, touching zero at the extremes.
  3. Option 1 shows a constant K.E. and option 2 a single sinusoid of period T dipping below its mean line; neither matches, so the answer must be option 3 or 4.
  4. The provided option image is cut off after option 2, so options 3 and 4 are not readable and no choice can be made.

Categories

AsksFigure readingread_diagramread a figure, graph or drawn structure and answer from it
ConceptKinetic energy in SHM goes as the square of the speed, so it never goes negative, touches zero at each extreme, and repeats twice in every period
Why this answerThis question requires matching the shape of a K.E.-against-time curve to the squared speed of SHM, demonstrated by all four options being K.E.-against-t plots, one of them 'a constant line'.
NoteThe four options reach this step as the placeholder text '[graph]'; I read them from `figure_image.text` and the coordinates in `figure_image.drawn.spec`, where option (1) is a horizontal line, (2) a sine about a non-zero dashed mean with period T, (3) two humps touching zero at 0, T/2 and T, and (4) a sine crossing below the axis. The printed shape is therefore four graph options, which the retired E1 vocabulary calls `graph_options`, not `plain_mcq` as the pattern decided. The live qtype list has no value for graph options and no field in which a `new_type` proposal could be carried on this axis, so I recorded `mcq` from the retired-vocabulary map and record the printed shape here; `asks: read_diagram` carries the graph-ness.
What catches a student
The trapoption 1Answers another questionanswers_other_questiontrue, and about this topic, but it answers something else

The constant line is the correct graph for the pendulum's TOTAL energy, so a student holding 'energy is conserved in SHM' plots the conserved quantity; kinetic energy is the part being traded away, and it falls to zero at each extreme.

Who fallsa student who has learnt energy conservation in SHM as the single line 'the energy stays constant in time'

Why it feels rightthe vertical axis is an energy axis and conservation is the headline result of the chapter

  1. okIn SHM the total mechanical energy does not change with time.
  2. badSo the energy plotted against t here is a horizontal line.The axis is labelled K.E., not total energy; what stays constant is K.E. + P.E., while K.E. alone swings between zero and the maximum.
Also pullsoption 4

Who fallsa student who writes the speed as v = v0 cos ω t and plots that same shape for the energy

Why it feels rightthe curve has the pendulum's own period T and passes through zero at the extremes, which is exactly where the kinetic energy does vanish

  1. okThe speed is zero at the extreme positions and greatest at the mean position.
  2. badSo K.E. follows the velocity curve, dipping below the axis on the return swing.K.E. goes as v2, so it can never be negative, and squaring the sine halves the period to T/2.
Also pullsoption 2

Who fallsa student who notices that the velocity curve must not go negative and lifts it above the axis instead of squaring it

Why it feels rightthe curve is positive everywhere and still carries the pendulum's period T, so it looks like a repaired velocity curve

  1. okK.E. cannot be negative, so the curve has to stay above the axis.
  2. badShift the whole sine up about a non-zero mean, keeping its period T.At each extreme position the bob is momentarily at rest, so the curve must come down to zero — and it does so twice per period, which makes the period T/2.

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. The circuit is a source vi in series with a diode D and a load R, i.e. a half-wave rectifier.
  2. During the half cycle that forward biases D, the ideal diode behaves as a short, so vD = 0 and the whole vi appears across R.
  3. During the other half cycle D is reverse biased, the current is zero, so there is no drop across R and the entire source voltage stands across the diode: vD = vi, a single half-sine.
  4. Hence vD must be a half-sine for one half period and flat zero for the other half period.
  5. Option 1 (|sin|, two humps of the same sign) and option 3 (-|sin|) are full-wave shapes a single diode cannot produce; option 2 is the undistorted sine, which would need a short in place of the diode.
  6. Only option 4 shows one hump followed by a flat zero, so it is the answer.

Consider two uncharged capacitors of equal capacitance 200 pF. One of them is charged by a 100 V supply and disconnected. Now this capacitor is connected to the uncharged capacitor. The amount of electrostatic energy lost in the process is:
  1. 0.5 × 10-6 J
  2. 1.0 J
  3. 1.0 × 10-6 J
  4. 0.5 J
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. Energy loss = 12C1C2C1 + C2V2
  2. = 12(200 × 200400) × 10-12(100)2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. Initial stored energy: Ui = 12CV2 = 12(200 × 10-12)(100)2 = 1.0 × 10-6 J.
  2. Initial charge: Q = CV = (200 × 10-12)(100) = 2.0 × 10-8 C; this is conserved when the second capacitor is connected.
  3. Equal capacitances share the charge equally, so the common potential is V' = Q2C = 2.0 × 10-8400 × 10-12 = 50 V.
  4. Final energy: Uf = 2 × 12(200 × 10-12)(50)2 = 5.0 × 10-7 J.

A uniform metallic wire having resistance 4 Ω is bent to form a square loop (ABCD) (see figure). A resistance of 2 Ω is connected between points B and D and a battery of 2 V is connected across points A and C as shown in the figure. Now the value of current (I) is :
  1. 2 A
  2. 8 A
  3. 4.5 A
  4. 4 A
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. → Each side will have resistance of 1 Ω
  2. → It is balanced wheat stone bridge
  3. → No current in the resistance of 2 Ω
  4. → [Reffective]AC = 1 Ω
  5. → I = EReff. = 21

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. The 4 Ω wire is uniform and bent into a square, so each of the four sides has resistance 44 = 1 Ω.
  2. The battery is across the diagonal A-C, and the two routes between them are A-B-C = 1 + 1 = 2 Ω and A-D-C = 1 + 1 = 2 Ω.
  3. These routes are identical, so B and D are at the same potential: the 2 Ω bridging them is a balanced-bridge arm and carries no current.
  4. The two 2 Ω arms are then simply in parallel: RAC = 2 × 22 + 2 = 1 Ω.
  5. I = VRAC = 21 = 2 A, which is option 1.

  2. Einduced = Bvl  [∵ →B ⊥ →V ⊥ →l ]
  3. = 0.3 × 2 × 10-2 × 3 × 10-2

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. The motional emf of an edge of length l moving with speed v perpendicular to a field B normal to the loop is ε = Blv.

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Four statements are given (A is mass number):

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
A.The volume of a nucleus is proportional to A1/3.
B.The volume of a nucleus is proportional to A.
C.The difference in mass of an atom and its nucleus is called the mass defect.
D.The difference in mass of a nucleus and its constituents is called the mass defect.
  1. A and C are true, but B and D are false
  2. B and C are true, but A and D are false
  3. A and D are true, but B and C are false
  4. B and D are true, but A and C are false
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. As we know,
  2. Size of nucleus, r = r0(A)13
  3. ⇒ r3 = r03 · A
  4. ⇒ V ∝ A  (∵ V = 43π r3)
  5. So, option A → wrong and B → correct
  6. while the difference between the actual mass of nucleus and its constituents is called the mass defect.
  7. ∴ option C → wrong and D → correct

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. The nuclear radius obeys R = R0 A1/3.
  2. Hence the volume V = 43π R3 = 43π R03 A is proportional to A, not to A1/3: statement B is true and statement A is false.
  3. The mass defect is defined as Δ m = [Z mp + (A-Z) mn] - Mnucleus, i.e. the difference between the nucleus and its constituent nucleons: statement D is true.
  4. The difference between an atom's mass and its nucleus's mass is just the mass of the orbital electrons (less their binding), not the mass defect: statement C is false.
  5. B and D true, A and C false is option 4.

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
In a metre bridge experiment (see figure), the positions of the cell, E, and galvanometer, G, are interchanged. We shall observe in the galvanometer:
  1. Only the left-sided deflection
  2. There will be no deflection irrespective of the position of the jockey
  3. Only the right-sided deflection
  4. Both right-sided and left-sided deflection and at balance point, no deflection
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. Position of null point will not change when galvanometer (G) and the cell (E) are interchanged.
  2. There will be no deflection in galvanometer only at balance point.
  3. In an unbalanced meter bridge, if E and G are interchanged mutually, then the deflection in galvanometer may be towards left-side or right-side.

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. A metre bridge is a Wheatstone network: R1 and R2 in the gaps, the two parts of the wire as the other arms, with the cell across one diagonal and the galvanometer across the other.
  2. Balance means the galvanometer diagonal carries no current, i.e. the two junctions are at equal potential; algebraically R1R2 = l100 - l.
  3. This condition is symmetric in the two diagonals, so interchanging the cell and the galvanometer leaves the balance point exactly where it was.
  4. Therefore the galvanometer still deflects one way on one side of the null point and the other way on the other side, with zero deflection at balance: option 4.

So swapping them leaves the balance condition the same. → Turn that into what you actually see as the jockey slides: deflection one way on one side of the balance point, the other way past it, and zero deflection where the condition is met.

Nothing in the circuit makes left different from right, so once you notice that you drop both on sight.

Without it, the natural guess is that the bridge no longer balances, which is option 2. The matching 'only left' and 'only right' pair cancels itself out. So everything depends on whether the balance survives the swap.
the catchThe whole question rests on one fact about the conjugate arms of a Wheatstone bridge, and nothing in the question points you to it. The figure gives you no numbers to fall back on.

Which of the following statements are correct?

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
A.Inside a conductor, the electrostatic field is zero.
B.Electric field at the surface of a charged conductor does not depend on its surface charge density.
C.The interior of a charged conductor can have no excess charge in the static situation.
D.At the surface of a charged conductor, the electrostatic field must be normal to the surface at every point.
E.The electrostatic potential is zero everywhere inside a charged conductor.
  1. A, B and D only
  2. A, C and E only
  3. A, C and D only
  4. C, D and E only
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. A. Electrostatic field is zero inside a conductor.
  2. B. Electric field at the surface of a charged conductor = σε0ˆn, depends on surface charge density (σ).
  3. C. The interior of a charged conductor cannot have any excess charge in the static situation.
  4. D. At the surface of a charged conductor, the electrostatic field ⊥ surface.
  5. E. The electrostatic potential is constant and can be non-zero everywhere inside a charged conductor.

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. A: in electrostatic equilibrium free charges have redistributed until the net field inside the conducting material is zero. True.
  2. B: just outside a charged conductor →E = σε0ˆn, which depends directly on the local surface charge density. False.
  3. C: by Gauss's law applied to any interior surface, the enclosed charge is zero, so all excess charge resides on the outer surface. True.
  4. D: any tangential component would drive surface charge along the surface, contradicting equilibrium, so the field at the surface must be normal at every point. True.
  5. E: the conductor is an equipotential, so the potential inside equals the surface potential - a constant, but not zero in general (a charged isolated conductor is at a non-zero potential). False.
  6. A, C and D only is option 3.

The surface field is proportional to the surface charge density. So 'does not depend' is the printed line with the dependence turned around. → Test E against 'potential is constant throughout the volume'. Constant is not the same as zero for a charged conductor. So E is the printed line with one word changed. → Confirm that A, C and D are each the exact printed property, put the three together, and find the option that matches.

  2. ⇒ λ > hcW0

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · medium
  1. A concave lens is a diverging lens, so an incident ray parallel to the principal axis bends away from the axis after refraction.
  2. The emergent ray therefore never crosses the axis; extended backwards, it meets the axis at the focus on the same side as the incoming light, so it only appears to diverge from that focus.
  3. Option 3 (emerges parallel) describes no refraction at all, and option 1 invokes a non-existent 2F rule for lenses, so both are out.
  4. Option 4 says the ray 'passes through' a focus, which a diverging lens ray never does - the focus is virtual.
  5. Option 2, 'appears to diverge from the principal focus', is the only statement matching the actual behaviour.

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Consider the following reaction :

2A(g) + B(g) → 2D(g)

Δ U⊖ = -10 kJ mol-1 and Δ S⊖ = -44 JK-1 at 298 K.

Identify the correct option with Δ G⊖ for the reaction and spontaneity of the reaction at 298 K.

(Given : R = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1)
  1. -1.635 kJ mol-1, spontaneous
  2. -0.63568 kJ mol-1, spontaneous
  3. +0.63568 kJ mol-1, non-spontaneous
  4. +1.635 kJ mol-1, non-spontaneous
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. 2A(g) + B(g) → 2D(g)
  2. Δ U° = -10 kJ/mol
  3. Δ S° = -44 J/K
  4. Δ H° = Δ U° + Δ ng RT
  5. Δ H° = -10 - 1 × 298 × (8.31)1000 = -10 - 2.48 = -12.48 kJ/mol
  6. Δ G° = Δ H° - TΔ S°
  7. = -12.48 - 298 × (-44)1000
  8. = -12.48 + 13.112
  9. = +0.632 kJ/mol
  10. Since Δ G° comes out to be positive, so given process is non-spontaneous.

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. Change in moles of gas: Δ ng = 2 - (2 + 1) = -1.
  2. Δ H⊖ = Δ U⊖ + Δ ng RT = -10000 + (-1)(8.31)(298).
  3. (8.31)(298) = 2476.4 J, so Δ H⊖ = -10000 - 2476.4 = -12476.4 J mol-1.
  4. TΔ S⊖ = 298 × (-44) = -13112 J.
  5. Δ G⊖ = Δ H⊖ - TΔ S⊖ = -12476.4 + 13112 = +635.6 J mol-1 = +0.636 kJ mol-1.
  6. Δ G⊖ > 0, so the reaction is non-spontaneous: option 3.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict

difficultyhard · 4 steps
stepsCount the change in the number of gas moles: 2 moles of product against 3 of reactant, so Dn = -1 → Change internal energy into enthalpy: DH = DU + Dn RT = -10000 + (-1)(8.31)(298) = -12476 J → Work out TDS = 298 x (-44) = -13112 J and subtract: DG = DH - TDS = -12476 + 13112 → Change the small leftover back into kJ and read its sign to say whether the reaction is spontaneous

the catchThe step students skip is turning DU into DH with the Dn RT term. If you skip it you get +3.1 kJ, which matches nothing. But if you get its sign wrong, or the sign of TDS wrong, you land exactly on the printed twin. And the answer is a small leftover from two large terms, so there is no rough size check available.

The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · medium
  1. Pick the longest continuous carbon chain; for this skeleton it runs through seven carbons, so the parent is heptane and names based on hexane (options 2 and 4) are wrong.
  2. The two branches on that heptane chain are one ethyl and one methyl, so 'diethyl' names are wrong.
  3. Numbering from either end gives the locant set {3,5}, a tie, so the rule is to give the lowest locant to the substituent cited first alphabetically.
  4. Alphabetically ethyl precedes methyl, so ethyl takes 3 and methyl takes 5, and the substituents are cited in that same alphabetical order.
  5. That gives 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane, option 1; option 3 is the same skeleton written with the locants and alphabetical order both wrong.

difficultyhard · 4 steps
stepsFind the longest unbroken chain in the drawing. It is seven carbons, not the six your eye follows first. → Number from both ends and compare the two sets of positions. They tie at 3 and 5. → Break the tie with the rule that the substituent that comes first alphabetically takes the lower number. So ethyl gets 3. → Put the name together with the substituents listed alphabetically.
confusing options3 of 4 · options 1, 2, 3
All four names are C10H22, and options 1, 2 and 3 all describe the same skeleton. Option 2 picks a six-carbon parent instead of the seven-carbon one. Option 3 is the correct chain numbered from the wrong end, which gives the same set of positions, 3 and 5. So the usual lowest-numbers check cannot reject it.
why it is trickyThis is hard not because it is long, but because the deciding rule is never signposted. The lowest-numbers test ties, and only the alphabetical tiebreak separates 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane from 3-methyl-5-ethylheptane. Meanwhile the wrong-parent-chain name sits there as a third live option for anyone who traces the drawn chain straight across instead of hunting for the longest one.
the catchYou need two naming rules, one after the other, and the second one, that the alphabetically first substituent wins a tie, is the one most students never learn. The wrong options are built on one broken rule each, not at random.

  1. (A) Molality = 2.560 × 100075 = 0.556 molal
  2. (B) Molarity = 540 × 1000450 = 0.278 M
  3. (C) Aquatic species are more comfortable in cold water
  4. Henry's Law KH ∝ Temp ∝ 1solubility
  5. (D) According to Henry's Law,
  6. P = KHX

  1. A: moles of ethanoic acid = 2.560 = 0.04167 mol, and the solvent mass is 75 g = 0.075 kg.

  3. B: moles of NaOH = 540 = 0.125 mol in 450 mL = 0.450 L.

  1. The half-cell reaction written as a reduction is 2H+ + 2e- → H2, so n = 2.
  2. Nernst equation: E = E° - 0.0592logpH2[H+]2 with E° = 0.
  3. HCl is a strong acid, so [H+] = 0.02 M and [H+]2 = 4 × 10-4.
  4. pH2[H+]2 = 24 × 10-4 = 5 × 103.

why this chapterThe answer turns on the formal charge count (valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus half the bonding electrons) for the three oxygen atoms of the ozone Lewis structure, giving 0, +1 and -1.
subtopic 1Octet Rule
why this subtopicThe answer depends on the formal charge count V - L - B/2 on the ozone Lewis structure: 0 on the doubly bonded terminal O, +1 on the central O and -1 on the singly bonded terminal O.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The correct formal charges on oxygen atoms numbered 2, 1 and 3 respectively are :
  1. -1, 0, +1
  2. 0, +1, -1
  3. 0, 0, 0
  4. +1, 0, -1
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. Formal charge = Valence electrons (V) - 12 (shared electrons) (S) - (non-bonding electrons) (L)
  2. Formal charge on 2nd oxygen atom = 6 - 12(4) - 4 = 0
  3. Formal charge on 1st oxygen atom = 6 - 12(6) - 2 = +1
  4. Formal charge on 3rd oxygen atom = 6 - 12(2) - 6 = -1

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. Formal charge = (valence electrons) - (lone pair electrons) - 12(bonding electrons), and each oxygen has 6 valence electrons.
  2. Atom 2 is the doubly bonded terminal oxygen with two lone pairs: FC = 6 - 4 - 12(4) = 0.
  3. Atom 1 is the central oxygen with one lone pair and three bonds (one double, one single): FC = 6 - 2 - 12(6) = +1.
  4. Atom 3 is the singly bonded terminal oxygen with three lone pairs: FC = 6 - 6 - 12(2) = -1.
  5. The charges sum to zero, as they must for neutral O3.
  6. Taken in the asked order 2, 1, 3 the answer is 0, +1, -1, which is option 2.

  1. 0.8 dm3 of CO, 0.8 dm3 of CO2

  1. CO2 + C(s) → 2CO
  2. 1
  3. 1 - x    2x
  4. 1 - x + 2x = 1 + x = 1.4

  6. Volume of CO2 = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6 dm3
  7. Volume of CO = 2 × 0.4 = 0.8 dm3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. The reaction over hot coke is CO2(g) + C(s) → 2CO(g), and the carbon is a solid so only the gases count in the volumes.
  2. Let x dm3 of CO2 react; by Avogadro's law it produces 2x dm3 of CO and leaves (1-x) dm3 of CO2.
  3. Total final volume = (1-x) + 2x = 1 + x.
  4. 1 + x = 1.4, so x = 0.4 dm3.
  5. CO formed = 2 × 0.4 = 0.8 dm3 and CO2 left = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6 dm3, which is option 2.

Identify the incorrect statement from the following :
  1. The largest and the smallest species among Mg, Mg2+, Al and Al3+ are Al and Mg2+ respectively.
  2. The IUPAC name of the element with atomic number 107 is Unnilseptium.

The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. The largest species is Mg and the smallest one is Al3+ among Mg, Mg2+, Al and Al3+.
  2. Unnilseptium element has atomic number 107
  3. Li and Mg are diagonally related and have similar properties.
  4. The oxidation state and covalency of Al in [AlCl(H2O)5]2+ are +3 and 6 respectively

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. Across period 3 the nuclear charge rises while the shell stays the same, so the neutral atom shrinks: Mg > Al.
  2. Both cations have the neon configuration, so the one with the higher nuclear charge is smaller: Mg2+ > Al3+, and both are far smaller than the parent atoms.
  3. The full order is Mg > Al > Mg2+ > Al3+, so the largest is Mg and the smallest is Al3+; statement 1 names Al and Mg2+ and is therefore wrong.
  4. Statement 2 is correct: 107 gives un-nil-sept-ium, Unnilseptium, in the IUPAC systematic naming of elements above 100.
  5. Statement 3 is correct: lithium resembles magnesium, the standard example of a diagonal relationship.
  6. Statement 4 is correct: in [AlCl(H2O)5]2+ aluminium is in the +3 oxidation state and is bonded to six donor atoms, so its covalency is 6.
  7. The incorrect statement is option 1.

printed in the booklet

READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Mixture of chloroform and acetone forms a solution with negative deviation from Raoult's law due to :
  1. Increase in escaping tendency of molecules of each component.
  2. Formation of hydrogen bonding between acetone and chloroform
  3. Stronger intermolecular forces between chloroform molecules than those between chloroform and acetone molecules.
  4. Repulsive forces.
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. Acetone and chloroform show negative deviation from Raoult's law due to stronger H-bonding between acetone and chloroform mixture.
  2. Hence, escaping tendency decreases
  3. ∴ Vapour pressure decreases
  4. ∴ Boiling point increases.

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. Negative deviation from Raoult's law means the observed vapour pressure is lower than predicted, which happens when the new A-B interaction is stronger than the original A-A and B-B interactions.
  2. The three electronegative chlorines of CHCl3 leave its single hydrogen strongly positive, so it can hydrogen bond to the lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen of acetone.
  3. This extra attraction holds the molecules in the liquid, lowering the escaping tendency and so the vapour pressure of both components, which is exactly negative deviation.
  4. That is option 2; option 1 describes positive deviation, and options 3 and 4 describe weaker A-B interaction, which would also give positive deviation.

    Which of the following statements are true with reference to the sex-determination in honeybees?

    Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
    A.An offspring formed from the union of a sperm and an egg, develops as a female (queen or worker).

    D.Males produce sperms by meiosis.
    E.Honeybees have a haplodiploid sex-determination system.

    3. A, B, C and D only
    4. A, B, D and E only
    The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
    1. In case of honeybees, males have half the number of chromosomes than that of females. The females are diploid, having 32 chromosomes and males are haploid, i.e., having 16 chromosomes. This is called as haplodiploid sex-determination system and has special characteristic features, such as, the males produce sperms by mitosis.

    → the working concludes: option 1

    printed solution, as in the booklet
    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
    1. A is true: NCERT Class 12, Ch. 5 states that in honeybees an offspring formed from the union of a sperm and an egg develops as a female (queen or worker).
    2. B is true: an unfertilised egg develops as a male (drone) by parthenogenesis.
    3. C is true: because the male arises from an unfertilised haploid egg, he has half the number of chromosomes (16) of the diploid female (32).

    5. E is true: this system, in which sex depends on the number of chromosome sets, is called the haplodiploid sex-determination system.
    6. So A, B, C and E only, option 1.

    1. NCERT Class 11, Ch. 5 (Morphology of Flowering Plants) gives marginal placentation, with ovules on the ventral suture ridge of a monocarpellary unilocular ovary, as that of pea, so A-II.

    What is the probability of having children with ‘O’ blood group, where both mother and father are heterozygous for ‘A’ and ‘B’ blood group, respectively?
    1. 25%
    2. 0%
    3. 75%
    4. 50%
    The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)

    2. ∴ The probability of having children with 'O' blood group will be 25%

    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
    1. A mother heterozygous for blood group A has the genotype IAi and a father heterozygous for blood group B has IBi (NCERT Class 12, Ch. 5, multiple allelism of the I gene).
    2. The mother's gametes are IA and i, each with probability 12; the father's are IB and i, each with probability 12.
    3. The four equally likely combinations are IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O).
    4. Blood group O requires the homozygous recessive ii, whose probability is 12×12=14=25%.
    5. Hence option 1.

    1. NCERT Class 11, Ch. 4 (Animal Kingdom) describes the Cyclostomata as ectoparasites on some fishes, with an elongated body bearing 6-15 pairs of gill slits for respiration and a sucking circular mouth without jaws.

    Choose the correct statements regarding muscle contraction.
    Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

    B.The neural signal generates an action potential which causes the release of Ca++ into sarcoplasm.

    E.Shortening of sarcomere takes place, by pulling actin filaments towards the centre of 'A' band.

    1. Statements A, B, D and E are correct while statement C is incorrect.
    2. A neural signal reaching neuromuscular junction releases a neurotransmitter (Acetylcholine) which generates an action potential in the sarcolemma. This spreads through muscle fibre and causes the release of Ca++ into the sarcoplasm. This Ca++ binds to the subunit of troponin on actin filaments and thereby remove the masking of active site for myosin on actin and hence facilitates the formation of cross bridge.

    → the working concludes: option 4

    printed solution, as in the booklet
    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
    1. A is correct: NCERT Class 11, Ch. 20 (Locomotion and Movement) states that muscle contraction is initiated by a signal sent by the central nervous system via a motor neuron, reaching the neuromuscular junction on the sarcolemma.
    2. B is correct: the neural signal generates an action potential in the sarcolemma which spreads through the muscle fibre and causes the release of calcium ions into the sarcoplasm.
    3. C is incorrect: the increase in Ca++ leads to binding of calcium with a subunit of troponin on actin filaments and thereby removes the masking of the active sites for myosin; it activates, not inactivates, the actin.
    4. D is correct: using energy from ATP hydrolysis, the myosin head binds to the exposed active sites on actin to form a cross bridge.
    5. E is correct: the cross bridge pulls the attached actin filaments towards the centre of the 'A' band, shortening the sarcomere.
    6. So A, B, D and E only, option 4.

    why this chapterThe answer turns on XO sex determination in grasshoppers, where males have 23 chromosomes and females 24.

    READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
    In a population of a grasshopper species, the chromosome number of some members is 23 and some other members possess 24 chromosomes. The 23 and 24 chromosome-bearing members in this species are ______.
    1. females and males, respectively
    2. all males
    3. males and females, respectively
    4. all females
    The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
    1. In grasshopper sex determination is XX - XO type, in which, males have only one X-chromosome besides the autosome (XO), whereas females have a pair of X-chromosome, besides autosomes (XX).
    2. Therefore, the individual with 23 chromosomes is a male grasshopper and the one with 24 chromosomes is a female grasshopper.

    → the working concludes: option 3

    printed solution, as in the booklet
    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
    1. NCERT Class 12, Ch. 5 (Principles of Inheritance and Variation) describes the XO type of sex determination, using the grasshopper as its example.
    2. In this type all eggs bear an X chromosome, while half the sperms carry an X and the other half carry none.
    3. An egg fertilised by a sperm with X gives a female with two X chromosomes; an egg fertilised by a sperm without a sex chromosome gives a male with only one X.
    4. So the male has one chromosome fewer than the female: 23 chromosomes in males and 24 in females.
    5. The members with 23 and 24 chromosomes are therefore males and females respectively, option 3.

    Option 1, Struthio, is the one that really competes. It is also the chapter's flightless bird, so you take it if you stop at 'flightless'. But the ostrich runs rather than swims, and its forelimbs are not paddles. Option 2, Neophron, is the vulture. Option 4, Psittacula, is the parrot. Both are strong fliers, so they die on the first word of the question.
    why it is trickyEasy. The question gives three cues: flightless, paddle-like forelimbs, swimming. Only one genus on offer satisfies all three. And two of the four options are ordinary flying birds, so they go before you recall any genus.

    why this chapterThe answer turns on the definitions of the interactions, mutualism benefiting both, parasitism benefiting one and harming the other, and amensalism harming one while the other is unaffected.

    printed in the booklet
    publisher’s solution, as printed
    READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
    Choose the correct statements regarding population interactions between two species.
    Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
    A.In both parasitism and commensalism, only one species benefits and the other species is harmed.
    B.Both species benefit in mutualism.
    C.Both species benefit in commensalism.
    D.In parasitism, only one species benefits and the other species is harmed.
    E.In amensalism, one species is harmed and the other is unaffected.
    1. B and E only
    2. A and B only
    3. B, D and E only
    4. A and D only
    The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
    1. In parasitism, one species is benefitted and the other is harmed. Whereas, in commensalism one species gets benefitted and the other remains unaffected.

    → the working concludes: option 3

    printed solution, as in the booklet
    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
    1. NCERT Class 12, Ch. 13 (Organisms and Populations) tabulates interspecific interactions by the sign of the effect on each species.
    2. B is correct: mutualism is (+,+), both species benefit.
    3. D is correct: parasitism is (+,-), one species benefits and the other is harmed.
    4. E is correct: amensalism is (-,0), one species is harmed and the other is unaffected.
    5. A is incorrect because it lumps commensalism with parasitism; commensalism is (+,0), so the second species is not harmed.
    6. C is incorrect for the same reason: in commensalism only one species benefits, the other is neither harmed nor benefited.
    7. So B, D and E only, option 3.
    printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
    33 highagree
    difficultymedium · 3 steps
    stepsPut up the sign table: mutualism +/+, parasitism +/-, commensalism +/0, amensalism -/0 → Check the five statements against it -- A wrongly folds commensalism in with parasitism, C gives commensalism a benefit to both, while B, D and E are as printed → Pick the option listing exactly the true set
    confusing options2 of 4 · options 3, 1 · long to execute
    Option 1 is the trap built on shared wording: statement A and statement D use the same 'only one benefits and the other is harmed' clause, so a candidate who rejects A for lumping commensalism into it can carry that rejection onto D and settle for B and E alone; option 2 is for whoever accepts A outright, and option 4 drops the one statement nobody doubts.
    why it is trickyMedium: five statements to check, but the interaction sign table is among the most thoroughly memorised pages in ecology, so the only real risk is the wording overlap between the false A and the true D rather than any gap in knowledge.
    the catchA false statement and a true statement share the same clause, so rejecting one can drag the other down with it.
